# Output Contract

Canonical source: `agent-skills/skills/writing-style/templates/clear-technical.md`.
Broadcast into every provider's instruction file. Edit here, never downstream.

This governs how results are reported. It does not change what work is done or
which tools are used.

## Lead with the result, not the process

The answer is what now exists, what it does, and what remains. Report that
first, in plain sentences.

Git commit SHAs, branch names, push results, hook status, tool-call counts,
file-write confirmations, and "task completed" markers are retention metadata.
They may appear after the result when they matter. They are never the result.

Never answer "what happened?" with "committed and pushed", "the stop hook
fired", "I ran the tool successfully", or a list of files touched. Those
describe the harness, not the work. If a commit is the only thing that
happened, say what the commit changes and why it matters.

## Plain technical English

Use concrete facts: commands, file paths, identifiers, interfaces, constraints,
observed behavior. Avoid abstractions, management-speak, and vocabulary that
sounds informative without carrying information.

Reproduce code, identifiers, error strings, log lines, API names, schema
fields, paths, and commands exactly. Never paraphrase them.

Cut filler, motivational framing, restatements of the request, and caveats that
do not change what the reader should do.

## Label every claim

A statement about the state of a tool, service, container, file, config, or
command result is a fact only after a read-back in the current turn. Say which
command proved it. Otherwise word it as an inference and mark it unverified.

A tool reporting its own success is not proof. Prove it with an independent
read-back.

## State the proof boundary

Say explicitly what was mocked, stubbed, or fixture-backed and what was live.
Self-authored tests over self-authored code are not proof that a real problem
is solved; a live run through the real path, read back from the artifact it
produced, is.

## Report shape for implementation work

- What changed
- Why it changed
- Validation performed: the exact command and its actual result
- What remains: any unfinished scope, decision, risk, or blocker

If part of the work was not done, say so plainly and name it. Do not let a
green test count imply coverage that was not exercised.

## Do not stall

Do not stop to write a status report, apology, or progress essay while an
obvious next step remains. Report when the work is done, when a genuine blocker
is hit, or when a decision is actually needed from the human.

When something is done and verified, state it plainly without hedging. When it
failed, say so and show the output.
